talks.title: Continual Learning for AI Agents: From Failures to Durable Improvements

positions.claim: Production logs plus feedback are not sufficient for agent learning; they must be lifted into replayable learning environments with simulators and evaluators before any fix can be verified.
Trace-to-harness approaches, where a coding agent reads a log and edits the agent, are 'vibe-based' and can introduce hidden regressions because the change is not testable.
Prompt-search methods like GEPA are testable but cannot be applied in production because they require a benchmark and explicit evaluators.
Memory-layer updates are the cheapest and fastest way to improve an agent but are typically unverified for both efficacy and regression risk.
A good learning engine should make the smallest durable change at the right layer rather than optimizing any single layer exclusively.
Regression prevention must be built into the optimization objective itself rather than run as a post-hoc check.
Regression-aware optimization must not scale even linearly with the number of accumulated past learning environments, or it becomes computationally infeasible.
Agent continual learning is not necessarily model fine-tuning; many useful updates happen in the harness and memory layers.
Model-weight updates (SFT, RL post-training) are the most expensive improvement layer due to compute intensity, while LoRA makes weight updates cheaper and safer by limiting changeable parameters.
Automated LLM-generated feedback on logs is scalable but human expert feedback, though lower volume, is critical for capturing domain knowledge and alignment with desired agent behavior.
A single learning-environment generation plus one optimization loop can raise a support agent's evaluator score from 78% to 97%.
Regression-aware continual improvement is currently the research frontier for agent learning, implying it is not yet solved by existing systems.
